definition: Document retrieval is defined as the matching of some stated user query against a set of free-text records.
details: These records could be any type of mainly unstructured text, such as newspaper articles, real estate records or paragraphs in a manual. User queries can range from multi-sentence full descriptions of an information need to a few words. Document retrieval is sometimes referred to as, or as a branch of, text retrieval. Text retrieval is a branch of information retrieval where the information is stored primarily in the form of text. Text databases became decentralized thanks to the personal computer. Text retrieval is a critical area of study today, since it is the fundamental basis of all internet search engines.

explainer.lead: Document retrieval is the task of finding text records that match what a user wants to know. It underpins internet search and also applies to collections such as manuals, newspaper articles, and real estate records.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a huge box filled with pages from newspapers, manuals, and other documents. You describe what you want, using either a few words or several sentences, and the system looks through the pages for ones that fit. It is like asking a librarian to fetch the right papers instead of reading the whole box yourself.
tiers.practitioner: A document-retrieval system accepts queries of varying specificity and matches them against mostly unstructured text records. Applications must accommodate both short keyword-like queries and multi-sentence descriptions of an information need. A useful check is whether the returned records actually address that need, rather than merely being part of the searched collection.
tiers.paperLevel: Let D be a set of free-text records and q a stated user query; document retrieval is the matching of q against D to identify records relevant to the information need. Records may range from newspaper articles and real estate records to paragraphs in a manual. Query length and specificity can vary from a few words to multi-sentence descriptions, and text retrieval is treated as a branch of information retrieval focused primarily on text.

explainer.example: A user searching a collection of manual paragraphs enters "How do I replace the ink cartridge?" The system matches that request against the paragraphs and returns the paragraph containing the cartridge-replacement procedure.

usedIn.detail: Individual paragraphs can be retrieved in response to a user's question.

usedIn.name: Newspaper archives
usedIn.detail: Articles can be matched against descriptions of an information need.

usedIn.name: Real estate record search
usedIn.detail: Mostly unstructured property records can serve as retrievable documents.

explainer.intuition: Instead of requiring a rigid question or a fixed record format, document retrieval compares a user's expressed need with free text. The central challenge is connecting queries of very different lengths and detail with relevant passages or documents.
howItWorks: Gather the free-text records that form the searchable collection.
Accept a query expressing the user's information need, from a few words to several sentences.
Match the query against the text records.
Return the records that match the stated need.
explainer.whyItMatters: Document retrieval makes large collections of unstructured text usable without requiring people to read everything. Its importance extends beyond specialized text databases because it forms the fundamental basis of internet search engines.
misconceptions: Queries do not have to be single keywords; they can be multi-sentence descriptions of an information need.
Document retrieval is not limited to complete articles or whole books; records can also be paragraphs in a manual.
Text retrieval is closely related, but it is the broader information-retrieval branch concerned primarily with information stored as text.
